Set up & run

Running unattended

Three ways to run goals, from you approving every gate to nobody watching, and the things that hold or stop a run.

In plain words

Start supervised. /sigma-goal does one goal and waits for your approval at every gate. When you trust it, /sigma-loop works through the backlog by itself and parks whatever needs a decision, then carries on. Nothing merges on its own until you switch work.auto_merge on, and a run is held back if the machine is short of memory and stopped when it hits a budget you set.

Which command

/sigma-goal/sigma-goal N --land/sigma-loop/sigma-orchestrate
Scopeone goalone named GitHub issue, only if the loop would pick itthe whole backloga batch of goals, as separate land sessions
At a checkpointpauses for youparks; the run endsparks to the review queue and continueseach session parks its own; the batch reports
Ends whenthe goal is done or you stopmerged, parked or failed (the final message says which)backlog empty, a budget, or a hand-off to a fresh sessionall waves are done or held

--land: one named goal, nobody in the loop

Built for starting one Claude Code cloud container per issue. It picks through the loop's own picker scoped to that issue, so the goal is taken only when /sigma-loop would take it: open, labelled sdlc:goal, not parked, blocked or in progress, no open prerequisite, no live claim by another run. It then runs the per-goal steps with no gate pauses and parks wherever the loop would park.

  • Refuses up front unless work.enabled is on and work.auto_merge is protected or always.
  • While it runs, no other goal is picked or written to. The named exceptions: the ledger watcher, issues the run files as follow-ups, and the release of the goal's own dependents when it closes.
  • Not measured: a run in a real cloud container. The behaviour is tested with fakes.

/sigma-orchestrate: a batch in waves

It decides what runs when, starts one --land session per goal, watches them through GitHub, merges what the post-PR review approves, unblocks dependents and reports. It writes no product code itself.

  • A wave is a set of goals that can run at once: every blocker inside the batch is in an earlier wave, and no two goals claim the same files. A goal with an outside blocker or a cycle is held, and so is everything waiting on it.
  • You get one go-ahead screen: waves, held goals, seats, where (--where cloud or local), model mix, merging on or off. --dry-run stops there and writes nothing.
  • Useful flags: --max-seats N, --no-merge, --model auto|sonnet|opus, --max-opus N, --yes.
  • Needs discovery.source: github, work.enabled, and work.auto_merge of protected or always.
  • Not measured: an end-to-end batch in a real cloud container. Its cost per merged goal is arithmetic from the code, not a measurement.

Merging: work.auto_merge

ValueBehaviour
off (default)Never merges. The pull request is left for a person.
protectedMerges only where the base branch genuinely requires checks or reviews, so GitHub's own gate does the refusing. On an unprotected branch it opens the pull request and says why it stopped.
alwaysMerges whenever the pull request is clean and safe, and says plainly that local verify was the only gate. It still stops when branch protection could not be read.

A goal is recorded done only when its pull request is confirmed merged. A fork, or a repository without write rights, never merges: it opens the pull request and records review.

What holds or stops a run

The resource guard

Sigma reads the machine (memory, load, pressure, cores) and derives its own limits, so a goal pick, a model session and a verify run each take a lease first. When there is no room the answer is a hold with a reason and a retry time: goals stay unclaimed, a verify exits without running, and the goal is not failed. The hold lifts by itself after consecutive healthy samples.

  • Modes: enforce (default), observe (logs the hold, admits), off. SIGMA_RESOURCE_MODE overrides the config key.
  • Under critical pressure only the verify process group that Sigma itself started is stopped. A model session is never signalled.
  • Not covered: tests you run by hand outside the verify wrapper, other programs' memory, the host's own subagent fan-out. On Windows the guard refuses rather than guess.
  • Uncalibrated: the five ratios are policy defaults. Two measured runs (macOS, and Linux in a 2 GiB container where an unguarded arm lost 2 of 4 verifies to the kernel and the guarded arm lost none) fixed none of them.

Budgets and hand-off

LimitStops the run when
budget.max_iterationsgoals admitted this session reach the ceiling
budget.max_minuteswall-clock minutes since the session's start reach it
budget.max_tokenspriced Claude-equivalent tokens reach it
budget.max_codex_raw_tokensmeasured Codex input plus output tokens reach it; checked at the next pick, so it does not count unmeasured turns
handoff.after_goalsthe orchestrating session has taken that many goals; it hands off to a fresh session

Each budget is per session and enforces only when set to a positive number. A stopped run is safe to resume: re-run it and it picks up where it left off.

Parking

The loop parks, it does not force. It parks on a decision only you can make, on an irreversible or expensive action (deploy, delete, overwrite, spend, migrate), and on a hard failure it cannot resolve (recorded as failed, distinct from parked). Parked goals collect in the review queue, which /sigma-status reports. The irreversible-action rule is an instruction to the agent unless you enable the hard-stop rulebook; see Trust and limits.

Overnight

A supervisor wraps the loop with no polling: it relaunches after a budget stop, sleeps until the stated reset after a usage-limit stop, and backs off after an unknown crash. Stop it with touch .sdlc/state/supervisor.stop. On a laptop run it under caffeinate -is, because a sleeping machine is not a sleeping process.

python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/supervise_daemon.py .sdlc
Headless runs need permissions pre-approved

In a headless mode the host cannot analyse the shell expansion the loop uses for its process id, and the call is denied. In one drill on a scratch repository, 3 of 5 loop runs worked around it and 2 stopped with nothing done. Supervised runs with "always allow" are the recommended path. For headless runs pre-allow the loop's own commands in a gitignored, per-machine settings file and pass a literal pid. Never add a wildcard delete to silence prompts, and do not run an unattended loop on a repository you do not trust.

Technical detail

Sources: running the loop, orchestrate, parallelism and the resource guard, running unattended, worktrees and merging. The compaction safety net, the supervisor's relaunch classes and the attended hand-off supervisor were measured in temp-directory tests only, not in a live compaction or a long unattended run.
